title: A Night at the Telescope, End to End
subtitle: Plan, expose, calibrate, measure and report one star, with a prepared plan: five stations, each with the number it hands to the next
body:
Step 1 of 11 read

Five stations

An observation is a chain. A plan says when a target is up and dark; an exposure is long enough to reach a signal-to-noise; a calibration turns counts into a magnitude; a measurement reads the counts from the frame; and a report gives the number with what it is good to. Each station is an instrument you have met, and each hands the next station one number.

This investigation follows a prepared plan: a star of magnitude 19 on the Las Cumbres 1.0 m telescope, on the night of 2025-01-29 (a new Moon), from a site at latitude 30° north. Every frame and every night of standard stars is synthetic, and the facility’s values are the instrument library’s; nobody has observed this. The first station is the night planner.

title: A Night at the Telescope, End to End
subtitle: Plan, expose, calibrate, measure and report one star, with a prepared plan: five stations, each with the number it hands to the next
body:
Step 3 of 11 question

A plan assumes clear nights

A plan for one night says nothing about clouds. The strategy planner of the observing-strategy investigations spreads three visits a night over a fortnight and draws the weather from a stated chain (60 percent of nights clear, with persistence). Read its Visits row: how many visits were executed of how many planned.

What share of the planned visits did the weather take, in percent?

%

title: A Night at the Telescope, End to End
subtitle: Plan, expose, calibrate, measure and report one star, with a prepared plan: five stations, each with the number it hands to the next
body:
Step 11 of 11 read

What you worked out

Station 1 found 8.1 usable hours at an airmass of 1.05 on a new-Moon night, and the strategy planner showed that a plan across nights loses 43 percent of its visits to a stated weather chain. Station 2 asked 59 seconds for a signal-to-noise of 50, limited by the star’s own photons. Station 3 calibrated against standards to 0.008 magnitude. Station 4 found the frame’s measured signal-to-noise within a draw of the prediction. Station 5 combined 0.022 and 0.008 into 0.023 magnitude, and the larger term, the star’s photons, is the one to improve.

Every frame and night here is synthetic and the facility’s values are the library’s; the chain is a prediction under stated assumptions, and it leaves out flat-field and sky-subtraction error, crowding, cloud and a changing atmosphere. The next investigation, From Photons to a Number, traces the arithmetic of stations 2 to 5 in one calculation.
